course.learn: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based test in which participants walk through a hypothetical incident or disaster and explain what they would do.
course.why: It reveals unclear roles, missing contacts, and plan gaps without risking production systems.
course.example: Leaders are told ransomware has disabled payroll and discuss notification, containment, recovery, and communications step by step.
course.exam: Talk through the scenario = tabletop. Actually performing simulated actions is a more hands-on simulation.

defs: Switching service from a failed primary system to a secondary system.

course.learn: Failover moves service from a failed primary resource to a secondary resource. It may be automatic or manual depending on architecture.
course.why: Failover is a core availability mechanism because a single failure does not have to become a service outage.
course.example: When the primary database becomes unhealthy, the standby replica is promoted and applications reconnect to it.
course.exam: Primary fails → secondary takes over = failover.

breakdown.explanation: Use duplicate components or paths so one failure does not stop the service.

Backups create recoverable copies of data or systems so organizations can restore after deletion, corruption, ransomware, or disaster. Good backup strategy considers location, frequency, retention, immutability, encryption, and restore testing.

course.learn: A simulation is a controlled exercise in which participants actively perform response tasks rather than only discussing them.
course.why: Hands-on practice tests tools, coordination, timing, and procedures more realistically than a tabletop.
course.example: A security team uses a lab environment to practice isolating hosts, restoring backups, and communicating during a mock ransomware event.
course.exam: Discussion only = tabletop. Performing controlled response actions = simulation.

Continuous operation

slides.teach: Study the order and purpose of each step. Process questions often ask what should happen next.

course.learn: Parallel processing uses multiple resources at the same time to distribute workload, improve throughput, and reduce dependence on one processing path.
course.why: It can improve performance and resilience when work can continue across multiple nodes.
course.example: A security analytics platform processes log streams across several worker nodes so one node failure does not stop all analysis.
course.exam: Parallel processing is about concurrent work; load balancing decides where work is sent; clustering coordinates resilient service nodes.
